dark_chocolate.title: Dark chocolate bars

produce_potatoes.title: Potatoes
produce_potatoes.question: Are organic potatoes worth it?
produce_potatoes.decision: Organic potatoes first; sweet potatoes carry far less residue.
produce_potatoes.why: Conventional potatoes carry a sprout inhibitor banned in the EU, on 90 percent of samples. Organic may not use it.
produce_potatoes.short_answer: Yes. Chlorpropham, a sprout inhibitor, was found on 90 percent of potato samples, and potatoes rank 37 of 47 for residue. Organic potatoes may not be grown with it; sweet potatoes are not treated with it.
produce_potatoes.detail: Potatoes rank 37 of 47 on the 2026 residue list, ordered from least residue to most. Chlorpropham, a sprout inhibitor banned in the EU, was found on 90 percent of samples, and the samples were washed and scrubbed before testing. Organic potatoes may not be grown with it, yet 12 of 28 organic samples carried residue, likely from storage alongside conventional potatoes. Sweet potatoes are not treated with chlorpropham; under 60 percent carried any residue, against 95 percent of potatoes. Store potatoes in a paper bag in a cool, dry, dark place.

deli_liverwurst_pate.decision: Pasture-raised liver, made with its own animal fat.
deli_liverwurst_pate.why: Liverwurst need only be 30 percent liver, with binders allowed. Traditional versions use pasture-raised liver and fat.
deli_liverwurst_pate.short_answer: Read the ingredients. Liverwurst must be at least 30 percent liver and may carry binders, extenders and mechanically separated meat. Choose liver from pasture-raised animals, made with animal fat rather than neutral oils.
deli_liverwurst_pate.detail: By federal standard, liverwurst and braunschweiger must contain at least 30 percent liver, and binders, extenders, mechanically separated meat and smoke flavoring are all allowed. seafood_fish_roe.title: Fish roe
seafood_fish_roe.question: Which fish roe should you buy?
seafood_fish_roe.decision: Salt-only roe, fresh or frozen; skip dyed lumpfish.
seafood_fish_roe.why: Fish eggs are a traditional sacred food, and fresh roe keeps with salt alone. Black lumpfish roe carries synthetic dye.
seafood_fish_roe.short_answer: Choose roe preserved with salt only, such as salmon roe, tarama or bottarga. Skip black lumpfish roe, which is dyed, and read shelf-stable jars for preservatives.
seafood_fish_roe.detail: Traditional food guides list fish eggs among the most prized foods and note roe is rich in vitamins A, D and K2, zinc, iodine and DHA. Roe comes fresh, frozen, smoked or dried. Most fresh caviars are preserved with salt only; shelf-stable caviars in boxes or glass may contain preservatives. Lumpfish roe, sold as a caviar substitute, is dyed with a synthetic black azo dye. Salmon roe is ikura; tarama is carp roe preserved with salt; bottarga is dried mullet roe. seafood_fresh_sardines_mackerel.question: Are fresh sardines and mackerel worth buying?
seafood_fresh_sardines_mackerel.decision: Fresh sardines or Atlantic mackerel; skip king mackerel.
seafood_fresh_sardines_mackerel.why: Small oily fish are high in omega-3 EPA and DHA and less likely to carry mercury. King mackerel is the exception.
seafood_fresh_sardines_mackerel.short_answer: Yes. Sardines and mackerel are high in EPA and DHA, and small fish are less likely to carry mercury or PCBs. King mackerel is the one to skip.
seafood_fresh_sardines_mackerel.detail: Sardines and mackerel rank high in EPA and DHA. Small fish low on the food chain are less likely to carry mercury or PCBs, and sardines are eaten whole with their tiny bones, which adds calcium and vitamin D. Most ocean fish carry more selenium than mercury; king mackerel and swordfish are the exceptions. Cooked fresh mackerel bones are too sharp to eat, unlike the softened bones in canned mackerel. Fresh sardines can be hard to find, so ask the counter.

seafood_trout.title: Trout
seafood_trout.question: Which trout should you buy?
seafood_trout.decision: Wild trout first; US farmed rainbow trout next.
seafood_trout.why: Traditional guides put wild fish first and farmed trout to avoid. Without wild, US farmed rainbow trout rates green.
seafood_trout.short_answer: Wild trout is the pick when stocked. US farmed rainbow trout, raised in freshwater raceways, ponds and net pens, is rated green and is the realistic fallback.
seafood_trout.detail: Traditional food guides place wild fish above farm-raised, and list farmed trout to avoid. All rainbow trout and steelhead farmed in the United States is rated green for environmental sustainability. US trout are farmed in freshwater net pens, flowthrough raceways and ponds; raceway waste is captured in settling ponds. Steelhead is the ocean-going form of rainbow trout. A serving supplies selenium, omega-3 fats and vitamins D and B12.

beef_veal.title: Veal
beef_veal.question: How do you choose veal?
beef_veal.decision: Pasture veal raised with its mother; skip white crate veal.
beef_veal.why: Calves raised on pasture with their mothers give light red veal. White veal comes from crates, banned in Europe.
beef_veal.short_answer: Choose veal from calves raised on pasture with their mothers, which is light red. Rose veal is pink. Pale white veal points to a crate system.
beef_veal.detail: Veal comes in three broad kinds. Vealers are calves raised on pasture with their mothers, and the meat is light red. Rose veal comes from calves reared in groups, some with pasture access, on milk or replacer and then grain, and the meat is pink. Crate veal is white because the calves are denied iron, a system illegal in the UK and Europe since 2007. Color is the counter clue.

poultry_chicken_wings.question: Which chicken wings should you buy?
poultry_chicken_wings.decision: Pasture-raised chicken wings, soy-free feed when the farm offers it.
poultry_chicken_wings.why: Wings and skin are the fattiest cuts, so feed shows most here. Soy-free pastured birds carry a better omega ratio.
poultry_chicken_wings.short_answer: Choose pasture-raised wings, and ask for soy-free feed. Wings are a fattier cut. Soy-free pastured chickens had a 3 to 1 omega-6 to omega-3 ratio, against 8 to 1 with soy.
poultry_chicken_wings.detail: Chickens are meant to range free, foraging bugs and greens; industrial birds are crowded, with little fresh air, on corn and soy feed. Fattier parts such as legs and wings carry more omega-6 than breast, and the skin is a concentrated fat source. Among pastured chickens, those fed soy had an omega-6 to omega-3 ratio of 8 to 1, against 3 to 1 for soy-free birds.
